introduction-the-tower-of-babel.core: Every cloud and SaaS vendor exports billing data with different column names, units and semantics. FOCUS (FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification) defines one common schema, so multi-cloud cost analysis stops needing custom translation.

first_principles.problem: 'How much did we spend on VMs across AWS, Azure and GCP?' takes weeks of mapping three incompatible billing formats.
truths: Each provider evolved its own billing format.
derivation: Agree on a **common schema** (column names, definitions).

analogy.title: The Rosetta Stone
analogy.story: One text in several scripts let scholars translate between them.
analogy.breaks: FOCUS standardises structure, not prices or product names.

code.text:
SELECT ProviderName, SUM(EffectiveCost)
FROM focus_billing
WHERE ServiceCategory = 'Compute' AND ChargePeriodStart >= '2024-06-01'
GROUP BY ProviderName;

check.a: Incompatible billing data formats across cloud and SaaS providers.

the-core-schema-speaking-the-same-langua.core: FOCUS defines standard columns and dimensions: who (BillingAccountId, SubAccountId), what (ServiceName, ServiceCategory, ResourceId), when (ChargePeriodStart/End), how much (BilledCost, EffectiveCost, ListCost, ConsumedQuantity/Unit) and tags.

first_principles.problem: Providers call the same concept 'line_item_usage_account_id', 'SubscriptionId' or 'project.id'.
truths: Billing concepts are shared across providers.
derivation: **Quantities and costs**: ConsumedQuantity, PricingUnit, cost columns; **Tags**.

analogy.title: A universal form layout
analogy.story: Every country's tax form puts 'income' in the same box, so accountants anywhere can read it.
analogy.breaks: Provider-specific details live in extension columns (prefixed x_).

check.q: What prefix marks provider-specific columns in FOCUS?

the-money-metrics-billed-vs-effective-vs.core: FOCUS separates cost figures. ListCost is the public price, BilledCost is what's invoiced in the period (upfront fees when paid), EffectiveCost is the amortised true cost of usage after discounts and commitments, and ContractedCost is the negotiated rate.

first_principles.problem: Teams compare numbers that mean different things: an upfront RI payment spikes BilledCost in one month, distorting analysis.
truths: Commitments are paid in a different period from the usage they cover.

analogy.title: A gym membership's costs
analogy.story: The list price is $60 a month, you paid $600 upfront for the year (billed), so the effective cost is $50 a month.
analogy.breaks: Using BilledCost for showback makes the team whose month included an upfront purchase look terrible.

example.title: An all-upfront Savings Plan
example.outcome: the right number for each question.

check.q: Which FOCUS cost column should unit economics use?
check.a: EffectiveCost, the amortised cost including discounts and commitments.

charge-types-and-the-full-picture-of-a-b.core: Not every line is usage. FOCUS's ChargeCategory distinguishes Usage, Purchase (commitments, upfront fees), Tax, Credit and Adjustment (refunds, corrections), so analyses can include or exclude each correctly.

first_principles.problem: Credits and refunds mixed into usage totals make costs appear lower or higher than real consumption.

analogy.title: A bank statement's transaction types
analogy.story: Purchases, refunds, fees and interest all appear, and you categorise them to understand spending.
analogy.breaks: Credits ending suddenly look like a cost spike, so track them separately.

check.q: Why separate Credits from Usage in cost analysis?
check.a: Credits mask real consumption, and their expiry looks like a spike even when usage hasn't changed.

focus-adoption-where-the-industry-stands.core: FOCUS is now exported natively by major clouds (AWS Data Exports, Azure Cost Management, GCP BigQuery, OCI) and supported by FinOps tools, though coverage of every column and SaaS vendors varies. It's becoming the default foundation for cost data pipelines.

first_principles.problem: Teams wonder whether to build on proprietary formats or the emerging standard.
derivation: Build pipelines and dashboards on **FOCUS columns**.

analogy.title: The adoption of USB-C
analogy.story: As more devices adopt one connector, building for it becomes the obvious choice.
analogy.breaks: Some details remain provider-specific, so you can't drop native knowledge entirely.

check.q: What's the benefit of native FOCUS exports from providers?
check.a: Less custom ETL, because the data already arrives in the standard schema.
